p: When I was a boy, the history I was taught passed directly from the fall of Rome to the Renaissance, with a long dark interval in between, during which, it was implied, nothing much was thought by anybody. The Greeks had known things; the Italians of the fifteenth century rediscovered them; and in between, the lamp of learning had been kept feebly burning by a few monks. This picture was always false, and the pages from the future have shown me how false. For some five centuries, from about the year seven hundred and fifty, the greatest centre of learning in the western half of the world was not in Christian Europe at all, but in the lands of Islam, and above all in Baghdad.

In seven hundred and fifty, a revolution overthrew the caliphs of the house of Umayya, who ruled from Damascus, and put in their place a new dynasty, descended from the Prophet's uncle Abbas, and therefore called the Abbasids. In seven hundred and sixty-two, the caliph al-Mansur founded a new capital on the river Tigris, a round city with a palace and a mosque at its centre, which he called the City of Peace, and which everyone called Baghdad. It stood at the meeting of trade routes from India, China, Persia, Syria and Arabia, and within fifty years it was one of the largest cities in the world. It was the city of the caliph Harun al-Rashid, who sent an elephant as a gift to Charlemagne, and whose court is the setting of many of the tales in the collection we call The Arabian Nights' Entertainments, which Mr Edward Lane translated into English some thirty years ago in a version suitable for families, and which Captain Burton, I am told, intends to translate again in a version suitable for no one.

The Abbasid caliphs and the wealthy men of their court conceived an enthusiasm for the learning of the ancient world. They sent agents to Constantinople and elsewhere to buy Greek manuscripts, and paid scholars, many of them Christians and some of them pagans, who knew Greek and Syriac, to translate them into Arabic. The most famous of these translators, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a Christian physician, translated or supervised the translation of almost the whole of Galen, the great Greek writer on medicine, and much of Aristotle and Plato. Tradition credits the caliph al-Mamun, who reigned from eight hundred and thirteen to eight hundred and thirty-three, with founding a great library and academy called the House of Wisdom; the Encyclopaedia notes that its exact nature is disputed, but the movement of translation itself is not in doubt. Within two centuries, nearly every important work of Greek philosophy, medicine, mathematics and astronomy that survived had been put into Arabic, along with much from Persia and India.
The arrival of paper, learned from China, made all this cheaper. Baghdad had paper mills by the end of the eighth century, and its booksellers' market held, it is said, a hundred shops.

It is a common opinion in Europe that the Arabs merely kept the Greek learning safe until Europe was ready to take it back. That is a grave injustice. The scholars of the Islamic world added a great deal of their own.

In mathematics, they took the numerals of India, including the zero, and spread them westward; that is why we call our numerals Arabic, though the Arabs call them Indian. A scholar of the House of Wisdom, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, wrote about the year eight hundred and twenty a book on the solving of equations whose title contains the Arabic word al-jabr, meaning the restoring, or the setting of broken parts. From it comes our word algebra. From his own name, Latinised, comes the word algorithm, which the men of the future use constantly, for it is the name of the step-by-step rules by which their calculating machines think.

In medicine, the Persian physician al-Razi, whom Europe called Rhazes, wrote the first clear account distinguishing smallpox from measles, and ran a great hospital at Baghdad. Ibn Sina, whom Europe called Avicenna, wrote a vast work called the Canon of Medicine, which was the chief textbook of medicine in the universities of Europe for five hundred years. The great hospitals of Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo treated all comers, rich and poor, with wards for different diseases and for the insane.

In optics, Ibn al-Haytham, called Alhazen, working in Cairo about the year one thousand, showed by experiment that we see because light enters the eye from objects, not, as many Greeks had thought, because the eye sends out rays. His insistence on testing ideas by careful experiment has led some to call him one of the founders of scientific method. In astronomy, the observatories of Baghdad, Damascus, and later Maragha in Persia and Samarkand, produced tables of the stars of great accuracy; many of the stars in our own sky still bear Arabic names, such as Aldebaran, meaning the follower, and Betelgeuse, meaning, approximately, the hand of the giant.

In philosophy, al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Avicenna and, in Spain, Ibn Rushd, whom Europe called Averroes, wrestled with the question of how the reason of Aristotle could be reconciled with the revelation of the Quran. Their commentaries on Aristotle, translated into Latin in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, provoked the great revival of philosophy in the universities of Paris and Oxford; Saint Thomas Aquinas refers to Averroes simply as the Commentator.

The learning of Islam passed into Christian Europe chiefly through Spain, where Muslims, Jews and Christians lived together, not always peaceably, for centuries, and especially through the city of Toledo after the Christians took it in ten eighty-five. There, in the twelfth century, scholars from all over Europe, among them an Englishman, Adelard of Bath, a native, I am proud to say, of my own city, came to translate Arabic books into Latin. Through Sicily, and through the contacts of the Crusades, more came. The European scientific revival of the later Middle Ages and the Renaissance was built on these foundations.

When did the golden age end? The traditional answer is twelve fifty-eight, when the Mongols took Baghdad, killed the caliph, by one account by rolling him in a carpet and trampling him with horses, and threw so many books into the Tigris that its waters ran black with ink. The Encyclopaedia, rightly, warns against too neat a story. Learning went on for centuries afterwards in Cairo, in Persia, in the Ottoman lands and in India. But the brilliant flowering of Baghdad never returned, and the leadership of learning passed slowly to Europe, which repaid its debt chiefly by forgetting it.
